# Counter-evidence

The case against, and the assumptions the research question smuggles in. Sources
in [citations.md](../citations.md).

## The framing problem

The question — "which countries are reasonable for a US investor to buy
residential property in and rent out" — presupposes three things:

1. **That some country is reasonable.** The grammar admits no null result. The
   honest possible finding, that none of the nine beats a US-domestic rental after
   costs, taxes, remote management and exit friction, cannot be expressed in the
   question's own terms.
2. **That obstacles are procedural.** "Nuances" and "hoops" frame a discretionary
   permit, a non-fee-simple trust, a licence with a legislated expiry date, and a
   200-metre statutory ownership bar as things to navigate. Several of them are
   not.
3. **That a comparable cross-country metric set exists.** It does not, in this
   corpus — see below.

## The missing comparison class

The nine countries are compared against each other and never against staying
home. Any ranking produces a winner even if the whole field is worse than the
domestic alternative.

**This corpus cannot make that comparison in either direction.** A search across
all 204 fetched files — 157 of which carry text — for yield and price-to-rent
terminology returned no rental
yield figure for any of the nine countries, and none for the United States. Every
price and rent statistical portal that was fetched returned a landing page, an
unexecuted query shell, or values rendered as images.

So the study can describe the rules precisely and cannot say whether the
investment pays, anywhere. That is a finding about the evidence base, and it is
the most important limitation in the whole document.

Three things do favour the domestic alternative, and all three are sourced:

- **Depreciation.** Domestic residential rental property runs on a 27.5-year
  recovery period; foreign property is forced onto ADS at **30 years**,
  straight-line, by IRC § 168(g)(1)(A) [48]. Identical property, identical
  taxpayer, smaller annual deduction purely because of location.
- **Estate exposure.** Six of the nine countries have **no US estate tax
  treaty** [45][46], leaving the § 2014 unilateral credit — capped by two ratio
  limitations, no credit for interest or penalties, a four-year claim window, and
  refunds paid without interest [49]. A domestic property carries none of this.
- **Reporting.** Directly held foreign real estate is not reportable, but held
  through a foreign entity the entity interest becomes a specified foreign
  financial asset valued inclusive of the real estate, with Form 8938 penalties to
  $60,000 and possible criminal exposure [47]. Mexico's restricted-zone trust and
  the corporate structures common in Costa Rica and Panama sit squarely in that
  path.

## Will the licence survive the hold period?

This is the best-supported counter-argument in the study, and it is supported
entirely from primary regulatory sources rather than from commentary.

- **Barcelona**: every tourist-flat licence lapses by **November 2028** under an
  enacted Catalan decree-law, and the future PEUAT will contain no category
  recognising the use, so "no existirà la llicència per a aquest tipus
  d'allotjament" [17][18]. A licence bought in 2024 has a legislated expiry inside
  a normal hold.
- **Greece**: the Athens freeze runs to 31 December 2026, is extendable **by
  administrative act** rather than new legislation, and **deletes the registry
  entry on any inter vivos transfer**, barring re-registration for the duration
  [25]. Buying a licensed short-let there destroys the licence.
- **Spain**: the national registry regime was annulled by three Supreme Court
  judgments about 16 months after entry into force, and under 11 months after its
  provisions took effect [15][16].
- **Italy**: the short-let volume ceiling fell from four apartments to **two**
  with effect from 2026, reclassifying a three-unit portfolio as entrepreneurial
  by operation of law [28].
- **Portugal**: the regime has been rewritten roughly every two years —
  DL 128/2014, DL 63/2015, Lei 62/2018, DL 9/2021, Lei 56/2023, DL 76/2024,
  DL 97/2026 [20][21].
- **France**: since 21 November 2024 a building's co-owners can amend the
  règlement to ban tourist letting in anything that is not a principal residence
  [24]. No legislature required.
- **Hungary**: the US income tax treaty an investor might have relied on for
  double-tax relief is **terminated** [50].

Six jurisdictions — Spain appears twice above, for the registry annulment and for
Barcelona — and seven documented instances of the operating rules changing under
an owner's feet, all within roughly three years.

## Obstacles that are structural, not procedural

- **Mexico**: no direct title in the restricted zone; a 50-year trust conferring
  no rights in rem; a discretionary public-interest standard; and a fine up to the
  entire transaction value for circumvention [5][6].
- **Costa Rica**: a statutory bar, not a permit, on non-resident foreigners
  holding a coastal concession, with the corporate workarounds explicitly closed
  and improvements forfeited without compensation on extinction [7].
- **Hungary**: a discretionary permit with a municipal-interest veto and
  **mandatory** refusal where public or municipal interest is harmed [3][4].
- **Spain**: 24% on **gross** rent with no expense deduction for a
  non-EU/EEA owner, against 19% on **net** for an EU owner [37] — an effective
  differential far wider than the headline five points.
- **Portugal**: a flat 7.5% IMT on non-residents with all reliefs disapplied,
  escapable only by relocating or accepting a capped rent for at least 36 months
  in five years [9][10].
- **Paris**: for anything that is not the owner's principal residence — the
  non-resident's position by definition — a change-of-use authorisation **with
  compensation**, meaning converting non-residential premises into housing, before
  the first night of letting [24]. That is a capital barrier, not a form.

## Where the academic evidence does not go as far as it appears to

The peer-reviewed study of foreign-buyer overpayment [60] is the strongest
academic source in the corpus and it does **not** support a residential
conclusion. Across roughly 28,500 transactions in eight countries, foreign
investors do pay significantly more — but in the property-type split the authors
state that outside industrial and office property, **including apartments**, "the
coefficients are insignificant", reasoning that information asymmetry is weaker
where values are easy to measure. The data are institutional transactions above
roughly US$1m, and **France is the only one of the nine in the sample**.

Reporting this as evidence that US buyers overpay for European homes would
misrepresent the paper. It is a directional caution about first-time cross-border
buying, nothing more.

The second academic source is commercial real estate and its body is paywalled
[61]; it notes chiefly that cross-border real estate "has seen little research".

**There is no study of realised net returns to cross-border residential
investment in this corpus.** The underperformance finding the brief asked for is
not available.

## Who publishes on this topic, and what that does to the evidence

The corpus is overwhelmingly composed of **tax authorities, tourism registries,
municipalities and EU institutions**. These sources tell you what you must do and
what you will be fined. They have no interest in, and publish nothing about,
whether the investment pays.

That is a structural bias with a specific consequence: **an optimistic conclusion
drawn from this corpus would be non-falsifiable**, because the evidence base
cannot produce a return figure that would contradict it. The regulatory detail is
excellent; the return evidence is absent by construction.

Two further interest notes:

- The two municipal sources are **advocates in an active political fight and say
  so**. Barcelona's page is a mayoral housing-plan press release; the Paris page
  opens by asserting that tourist letting reduces private rental supply and raises
  housing costs [18][24]. That does not make their statements of law wrong — the
  2028 expiry and the compensation requirement *are* the law — but their
  forward-looking claims are political projections.
- The main French enforcement dataset comes from **the profession paid to
  enforce** [30]. The Chambre nationale des commissaires de justice counts acts
  its own members serve, and the same document tracks five bills including one
  "visant à défendre les propriétaires victimes d'impayés locatifs". Its
  first-party counts are sound; its comparative European figures and squat
  estimates are third-party and were not verified. To its credit it flags its own
  gaps — "il n'existe pas de chiffre officiel", "Il n'existe pas de statistiques
  consolidées sur le nombre de squats".

## Counter-arguments that are plausible and are NOT supported here

Listed explicitly so they are not mistaken for findings. Each is a **concern**:

1. **Currency risk** on USD-funded, EUR/HUF/MXN/CRC-denominated cash flows. The
   corpus has a single dated FX rate [52] and no volatility series.
2. **Mortgage availability and pricing** for a non-resident US buyer, including
   whether FATCA compliance costs deter foreign banks. Nothing.
3. **Forced heirship** and civil-law succession overriding a US will. Nothing.
4. **Whether a Mexican fideicomiso is a foreign trust** for Forms 3520/3520-A.
   Nothing — and for a restricted-zone purchase this is the largest unexamined
   US-side risk in the study.
5. **Vacancy and turnover cost** for an absentee owner. Only census unoccupancy
   definitions exist [58], which are a different quantity.
6. **Enforcement intensity** — how often the Spanish gross-basis rule, the Greek
   €20,000 minimum fine or the Paris €1,000/day/m² astreinte is actually applied.
   Barcelona's ~300 complaints per month [18] is the only enforcement-volume datum
   in the corpus.
7. **Whether the European restrictions represent a directional trend** rather
   than three coincident local actions. The direction is consistent across every
   European regulatory file here, but "trend" is inference; no source characterises
   it as one.
